\chapter{The Past That Takes To Be}
\label{ch:ge-perfekt-sein}
\hlchaptermodality{18}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can build the German past of verbs of motion and change with the verb for “to be” instead of the verb for “to have”, and say why the participle never changes.}

Motion and change of state build their perfect on sein rather than haben — ich bin gegangen beside ich habe gelernt. The chapter teaches the rule, then the four verbs that follow it (kommen, fahren, werden, bleiben), then the short list that has to be learned outright, and finally the one place German is simpler than French: the participle in the perfect agrees with nothing at all.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ich bin gegangen]{ich bin gegangen — the perfect built on sein}

\label{lesson:GE-C16-perfekt-sein}



\begin{quote}
You built the everyday past with \emph{haben} — \textbf{ich habe gelernt}. A particular family of verbs refuses \emph{haben} and takes this chapter's verb instead.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: which verbs take sein}]
\begin{quote}
Verbs of \textbf{motion} and \textbf{change of state} build their perfect with \textbf{sein}, not \emph{haben}.
\end{quote}

An action that leaves you somewhere else, or leaves you something else, takes \emph{sein}. An ordinary activity that leaves you where you were keeps \emph{haben}: \emph{ich habe gearbeitet}, \emph{ich habe getanzt}.

\emph{Gehen} is the model, and because every present form of \emph{sein} now belongs to you, the whole thing reads off without a single new word:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{German} & \textbf{English} \\
\midrule
\emph{ich \textbf{bin} gegangen} & I went / I have gone \\
\emph{du \textbf{bist} gegangen} & you went \\
\emph{er \textbf{ist} gegangen} & he went \\
\emph{wir \textbf{sind} gegangen} & we went \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The recipe is the one you already know, with the helper swapped:

\begin{quote}
present form of \textbf{sein} + past participle, and the participle goes \textbf{last}
\end{quote}
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{ge-prefix} — \emph{gegangen} opens with the same unstressed \textbf{ge-} that wrapped \emph{gelernt} and \emph{gesagt}. It is never stressed; the weight falls on \emph{-gang-}.
  \item \texttt{ich-laut} — and \emph{ich} keeps its soft ending right before it, so the phrase runs \emph{ich bin ge-GANG-en} without a break.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ich bin gegangen; du bist gegangen; er ist gegangen; wir sind gegangen\textquotedblright{}
  \item the contrast — \textquotedblleft{}ich habe gelernt … ich bin gegangen\textquotedblright{}
  \item the rule — \textquotedblleft{}motion and change take sein\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}ich bin gegangen.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which family of verbs takes \emph{sein}? (\textbf{Motion and change of state}.) Say \textquotedblleft{}I went.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Ich bin gegangen}.) Where does the participle sit? (\textbf{At the end}.) Which helper does \emph{arbeiten} take? (\emph{\textbf{Haben}} — it is an activity, not a change.) Next: the first of the family, and it is the one you say most.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kommen]{kommen — \textquotedblleft{}to come\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C16-kommen}



\begin{quote}
Motion takes \emph{sein}. Here is the motion verb you will use as often as \emph{gehen}, and it is an English word you already own.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: kommen}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{kommen} — \textquotedblleft{}to come.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{ich bin gekommen} — \textquotedblleft{}I came.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

The infinitive wears the \textbf{-en} you know. The participle is \textbf{gekommen}: the \emph{ge-} wrap in front, and \emph{-en} rather than \emph{-t} at the back, because this is one of the old strong verbs rather than a regular one.

Coming is arriving somewhere you were not. That is motion with a result, so it takes \emph{sein}, exactly as \emph{gehen} does.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{kommen} and English \textbf{come} are the same word, both from Germanic \textbf{*\emph{kwemaną}}. No Latin anywhere in the line — French \emph{venir} and Spanish \emph{venir} come from Latin \emph{venīre} instead, which is where English gets \emph{advent}, \emph{convene} and \emph{venue}.

So English, as usual, owns both halves: the everyday \textbf{come} from the Germanic side, the formal \textbf{convene} from the Latin.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{vowel-o} — the \textbf{o} is short and open, the vowel of English \emph{cot}, not the \emph{uh} English puts in \emph{come}.
  \item \texttt{ge-prefix} — \emph{gekommen} keeps the unstressed \textbf{ge-}; the stress is on \emph{-KOMM-}.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}kommen\textquotedblright{} — short open \emph{o}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ich bin gekommen\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ich bin gegangen … ich bin gekommen\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}ich bin gekommen.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{kommen} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{To come}.\textquotedblright{}) Say \textquotedblleft{}I came.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Ich bin gekommen}.) Which helper, and why? (\emph{\textbf{Sein}} — it is motion.) Which English word is it? (\textbf{Come}.) Next: the verb that covers everything with a vehicle under it.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[fahren]{fahren — \textquotedblleft{}to travel, to drive\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C16-fahren}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Gehen} is going on your feet. When there is a vehicle under you, German changes the verb.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: fahren}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{fahren} — \textquotedblleft{}to travel, to go by vehicle, to drive.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{ich bin gefahren} — \textquotedblleft{}I travelled, I drove.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

German keeps two verbs where English makes do with \emph{go}. You \textbf{gehen} on foot and you \textbf{fahren} in anything with wheels — a car, a bus, a train, a bicycle. Getting that pair right is one of the first things that makes a learner sound German rather than translated.

It is motion, so the helper is \emph{sein}.

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{vowel-a-long} — the \textbf{a} is long and open, as in \emph{war}.
  \item \texttt{h-silent-lengthening} — and the \textbf{h} after it is the silent stretcher you met in \emph{gehen} and \emph{sehen}: it is not breathed, it only holds the vowel. \emph{FAH-ren} rhymes with the way \emph{gehen} and \emph{sehen} are built.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{fahren} is English \textbf{fare} — the old verb meaning \textquotedblleft{}to travel,\textquotedblright{} which English demoted to a noun and then almost forgot. It is still there in:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{English word} & \textbf{what it is really saying} \\
\midrule
\textbf{farewell} & travel well \\
\textbf{thoroughfare} & a way you can travel through \\
\textbf{seafaring} & sea-travelling \\
the \textbf{fare} you pay & what the travelling costs \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

So \emph{auf Wiedersehen} and \emph{farewell} are built the same way: both are a wish handed over at the door, one about seeing again, one about travelling well.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}fahren\textquotedblright{} — long \emph{a}, silent \emph{h}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ich bin gefahren\textquotedblright{}
  \item the pair — \textquotedblleft{}gehen on foot, fahren with wheels\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}fahren — fare — farewell\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}Ich bin gefahren.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{fahren} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{To travel, to go by vehicle}.\textquotedblright{}) Which verb would you use walking to the shop? (\emph{\textbf{Gehen}}.) Say \textquotedblleft{}I drove.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Ich bin gefahren}.) Which English word is \emph{fahren}? (\textbf{Fare} — as in \emph{farewell}.) Next: the verb for becoming something else.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[werden]{werden — \textquotedblleft{}to become\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C16-werden}



\begin{quote}
The rule has two halves. \emph{Gehen}, \emph{kommen} and \emph{fahren} are the motion half. This one word is the whole of the other half.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: werden}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{werden} — \textquotedblleft{}to become.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{ich bin geworden} — \textquotedblleft{}I became.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\emph{Sein} says what you are. \emph{Werden} says what you turn into. Where \emph{sein} sits still, \emph{werden} moves — and that is exactly why it takes \emph{sein} as its helper: becoming is change of state in its purest form.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Ich bin müde geworden.} — \textquotedblleft{}I got tired.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Notice what that sentence does. The adjective you learned with \emph{sein} now describes an arrival rather than a condition. German makes the difference with the verb; English does it with \emph{be} against \emph{get}.

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{w-as-v} — the \textbf{w} is English \textbf{v}, as in \emph{war} and \emph{wir}.
  \item \texttt{d-t-final} — and in \textbf{wird} (\textquotedblleft{}he becomes\textquotedblright{}) the final \textbf{d} devoices to a \textbf{t}, the same rule that turned \emph{sind} into \emph{zint}.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{werden} is a lost English verb — \emph{weorthan}, \textquotedblleft{}to turn, to come to be\textquotedblright{} — and its bones are still in the language:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{English} & \textbf{the buried meaning} \\
\midrule
to\textbf{ward} & turning to \\
back\textbf{ward} & turning back \\
\textbf{worth} & what a thing turns out to be \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

So \emph{werden} means \textquotedblleft{}to turn into,\textquotedblright{} and every time you say \emph{toward} you are using the same root without knowing it.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}werden\textquotedblright{} — \emph{VAIR-den}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ich bin geworden\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Ich bin müde geworden.\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}I got tired\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}werden — toward — worth\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}Ich bin müde geworden.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{werden} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{To become}.\textquotedblright{}) Why does it take \emph{sein}? (\textbf{It is change of state} — the other half of the rule.) Say \textquotedblleft{}I became.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Ich bin geworden}.) Which English words hide the same root? (\emph{\textbf{Toward}}, \emph{\textbf{backward}}, \emph{\textbf{worth}}.) Next: the two verbs that break the rule by standing still.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bleiben]{bleiben — \textquotedblleft{}to stay\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C16-bleiben}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Werden} takes \emph{sein} because it is pure change. This verb takes \emph{sein} too — and it means staying exactly where you are.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: bleiben}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{bleiben} — \textquotedblleft{}to stay, to remain.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{ich bin geblieben} — \textquotedblleft{}I stayed.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

By the rule as stated, this verb should take \emph{haben}. Staying is not motion and it is not change; it is the absence of both. It takes \emph{sein} anyway, and every German learner meets it as a fact rather than a consequence.

The honest way to hold it: \emph{bleiben} is on the \emph{sein} list because it is about \textbf{where you are} rather than \textbf{what you do}, and that is the deeper thing the motion rule was pointing at all along.

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{diphthong-ei} — \textbf{ei} is the \emph{eye} vowel again, exactly as in \emph{sein}. So \emph{bleiben} is \emph{BLY-ben}, never \emph{blee-ben}. The two verbs of this chapter that break the rule both carry that vowel.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{bleiben} is \textbf{be-} plus an old Germanic verb \emph{lība-}, \textquotedblleft{}to remain.\textquotedblright{} English lost the verb and kept its leavings — literally: what \textbf{remains} after everything else has gone is what English calls the \textbf{leftovers}, and \emph{leave} in the sense of \emph{what is left} belongs to the same family.

German still uses the verb every day; English kept only the residue of it, which is a fitting fate for a word meaning \textquotedblleft{}to be left over.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}bleiben\textquotedblright{} — \emph{BLY-ben}, the \emph{eye} vowel
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ich bin geblieben\textquotedblright{}
  \item the odd pair — \textquotedblleft{}ich bin geworden … ich bin geblieben\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}Ich bin geblieben.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{bleiben} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{To stay}.\textquotedblright{}) Say \textquotedblleft{}I stayed.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Ich bin geblieben}.) Does the motion rule predict its helper? (\textbf{No} — it has to be learned.) How is \emph{ei} pronounced? (Like English \textbf{eye}.) Next: the rest of the verbs that have to be learned, including this chapter's own verb.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ich bin gewesen]{ich bin gewesen — and the rest of the learned list}

\label{lesson:GE-C16-perfekt-sein-ausnahmen}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Bleiben} was the first verb the rule failed to predict. Here is the whole of the rest of that list, and it is short.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the verbs you simply learn}]
\begin{quote}
Besides motion and change, a small fixed set of verbs takes \emph{sein} and has to be \textbf{learned}.
\end{quote}

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{verb} & \textbf{perfect} & \textbf{meaning} \\
\midrule
\emph{sein} & \emph{ich bin \textbf{gewesen}} & I have been \\
\emph{bleiben} & \emph{ich bin \textbf{geblieben}} & I stayed \\
\emph{gelingen} & \emph{es ist \textbf{gelungen}} & it succeeded \\
\emph{geschehen} & \emph{es ist \textbf{geschehen}} & it happened \\
\emph{passieren} & \emph{es ist \textbf{passiert}} & it happened \\
\emph{begegnen} & \emph{ich bin \textbf{begegnet}} & I met \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{Sein} and \emph{bleiben} head the list because they are the two that most clearly contradict the rule: one says a thing simply is, the other says it stays. The rest are events that arrive of their own accord — succeeding, happening, running into somebody — and German treats an arrival as a change.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Look closely at \textbf{gewesen}. Strip the \emph{ge-} wrap and the \emph{-en} ending and what is left is \emph{\textbf{wes-}} — the third of the three roots inside this verb, the one that gave \emph{war} and English \emph{was}.

So \emph{sein} reaches for that root twice: once for its past tense, once for its participle. The infinitive comes from one root, the present from two, the past and participle from a third. There is no part of this verb that belongs to all of it.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ich bin gewesen; ich bin geblieben\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}es ist passiert\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}it happened\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}war … gewesen\textquotedblright{} — the same root twice
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}ich bin gewesen.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Name the two verbs at the head of the learned list. (\emph{\textbf{Sein}} and \emph{\textbf{bleiben}}.) Say \textquotedblleft{}I have been.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Ich bin gewesen}.) Say \textquotedblleft{}it happened.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Es ist passiert} — or \emph{es ist geschehen}.) Which root is hiding inside \emph{gewesen}? (\textbf{*\emph{wes-}}, the one behind \emph{war}.) Next: the ending German does not put on any of these.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[gegangen]{gegangen — the participle that never changes}

\label{lesson:GE-C16-perfekt-sein-agreement}



\begin{quote}
French draws the same \emph{have}-against-\emph{be} line German does. Here is the place the two languages part company, and German comes out easier.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: German agrees with nothing here}]
\begin{quote}
Inside the perfect, the German participle takes \textbf{no ending at all}. \emph{Gegangen} is \emph{gegangen} for every person, number and gender.
\end{quote}

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{French} & \textbf{German} \\
\midrule
he went & \emph{il est \textbf{allé}} & \emph{er ist \textbf{gegangen}} \\
she went & \emph{elle est \textbf{allée}} & \emph{sie ist \textbf{gegangen}} \\
they went & \emph{ils sont \textbf{allés}} & \emph{sie sind \textbf{gegangen}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

French makes the participle agree with its subject and spells the agreement out three different ways. German changes the helper — \emph{ist}, \emph{sind} — and leaves the participle exactly where it found it.

Old High German did inflect it here, at least some of the time. Modern German lost that, along with most of its other adjective-like endings in this position. So the simplicity is not a design; it is an erosion, and German happens to have come out ahead.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
It would be easy to assume German copied this split from Latin, the way it borrowed so much else. It did not.

The \emph{haben}-perfect and the \emph{sein}-perfect are \textbf{native Germanic developments}. They grew up alongside the Romance ones rather than out of them: neighbouring languages drifting the same way over centuries of contact, the same areal spread that pushed the simple past out of everyday speech in French, German and Italian together.

Two things to carry forward, and they point in opposite directions:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the \textbf{split} between the two helpers is shared with French;
  \item the \textbf{agreement} is not.
\end{itemize}
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}er ist gegangen; sie ist gegangen; sie sind gegangen\textquotedblright{}
  \item the participle, unchanged, three times — \textquotedblleft{}gegangen, gegangen, gegangen\textquotedblright{}
  \item the comparison — \textquotedblleft{}elle est allée … sie ist gegangen\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}sie ist gegangen; sie sind gegangen.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Does the German participle agree with its subject in the perfect? (\textbf{No} — never.) What changes instead? (\textbf{The helper} — \emph{ist}, \emph{sind}.) Does French agree? (\textbf{Yes}.) Did German take this split from Latin? (\textbf{No} — it grew in parallel.) Next: the one place a German participle does take an ending.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[der angekommene Zug]{der angekommene Zug — where the ending comes back}

\label{lesson:GE-C16-partizip-attributiv}



\begin{quote}
The participle takes no ending in the perfect. That is a fact about the perfect, not about participles — and the difference matters.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: in front of a noun, it inflects}]
\begin{quote}
A German participle standing \textbf{in front of a noun} is working as an adjective, and it takes the endings adjectives take there.
\end{quote}

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{German} & \textbf{English} \\
\midrule
\emph{ein geschrieben\textbf{er} Brief} & a written letter \\
\emph{der angekommen\textbf{e} Zug} & the arrived train \\
\emph{die eingeschlafen\textbf{e} Katze} & the fallen-asleep cat \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Each noun keeps its capital, and each participle now carries a small ending chosen by the article in front of it. That is the ordinary German adjective machine, applied to a participle. (\emph{Katze}, \textquotedblleft{}cat\textquotedblright{}, gets a lesson of its own later; here it is only carrying the ending.)

So German did not lose participle endings everywhere. It lost them in exactly one construction: the perfect.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{ge-prefix} — all three participles above still carry their \textbf{ge-} wrap, and it is still unstressed. In \emph{angekommen} it has slid into the middle of the word, behind \emph{an-}, which is where German puts it when a prefix comes first.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}der angekommene Zug\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}die eingeschlafene Katze\textquotedblright{}
  \item the contrast — \textquotedblleft{}sie ist gegangen\textquotedblright{} (no ending) … \textquotedblleft{}die eingeschlafene Katze\textquotedblright{} (ending)
  \item \textquotedblleft{}die müde Mutter\textquotedblright{} — an ordinary adjective doing the same thing
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where does a German participle still take an ending? (\textbf{In front of a noun}, as an adjective.) Where does it never take one? (\textbf{In the perfect}.) Say \textquotedblleft{}the arrived train.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Der angekommene Zug}.) What is the participle behaving as, in that phrase? (\textbf{An adjective}.) Next: choosing between the two helpers, on the spot.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — haben or sein?}

\label{lesson:GE-C16-haben-oder-sein}



\begin{quote}
No new words. The only skill left in this chapter is picking the right helper without stopping to think, and that is drill.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the whole family in one place}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{verb} & \textbf{perfect} & \textbf{why} \\
\midrule
\emph{gehen} & \emph{ich bin gegangen} & motion \\
\emph{kommen} & \emph{ich bin gekommen} & motion \\
\emph{fahren} & \emph{ich bin gefahren} & motion \\
\emph{werden} & \emph{ich bin geworden} & change of state \\
\emph{bleiben} & \emph{ich bin geblieben} & learned \\
\emph{sein} & \emph{ich bin gewesen} & learned \\
\emph{lernen} & \emph{ich \textbf{habe} gelernt} & ordinary activity \\
\emph{machen} & \emph{ich \textbf{habe} gemacht} & ordinary activity \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Read the right-hand column and you can see how much of the work the motion rule does on its own: only two rows have to be memorised outright.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{The exchange}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{German} & \textbf{English} \\
\midrule
\emph{Wo bist du gewesen?} & Where have you been? \\
\emph{Ich bin nach Berlin gefahren.} & I travelled to Berlin. \\
\emph{Und Anna? Ist sie gekommen?} & And Anna? Did she come? \\
\emph{Anna ist zu Hause geblieben.} & Anna stayed at home. \\
\emph{Ich habe viel gelernt. Jetzt bin ich müde.} & I learned a lot. Now I am tired. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Note the third and fourth lines: \emph{ist sie gekommen}, \emph{Anna ist geblieben} — a feminine subject both times, and not one letter added to either participle.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the contrast pair — \textquotedblleft{}ich habe gelernt … ich bin gegangen\textquotedblright{}
  \item the family — \textquotedblleft{}bin gekommen, bin gefahren, bin geworden, bin geblieben, bin gewesen\textquotedblright{}
  \item the French comparison — \textquotedblleft{}elle est allée … sie ist gegangen\textquotedblright{}, no ending at all
  \item the one place the ending returns — \textquotedblleft{}der angekommene Zug\textquotedblright{}
  \item the whole exchange, both voices
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}ich habe gelernt … ich bin gegangen.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built — where this volume pauses}]
You have gone from \emph{guten Tag} to two working past tenses, and the method has not changed once: take the word apart, find the English cousin sleeping inside it, and let the family tree do the memorising for you.

The next volume picks the thread back up with describing what you see.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which helper for \emph{tanzen}, \textquotedblleft{}to dance\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{\textbf{Haben}} — an activity.) Which for \emph{fahren}? (\emph{\textbf{Sein}} — motion.) Which two verbs on the \emph{sein} list mean the opposite of change? (\emph{\textbf{Sein}} and \emph{\textbf{bleiben}}.) Say \textquotedblleft{}she stayed.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Sie ist geblieben} — no ending on the participle.)
\end{tcolorbox}
